meta.note: Module copy: the research question, instructions, feedback and report scaffolding. Editable without touching JavaScript (standards 3.4).

researchQuestion.text: How abundant is Meadow Butterweed across Ashcombe Meadow?
researchQuestion.hypothesisPrompt: Choose your hypothesis before you sample.
meadowFacts: The meadow is 100 m × 100 m (one hectare).
The low ground near the stream (west edge) is wet; the rise to the east is dry.
Five species dominate: Meadow Butterweed, Common Daisy-leaf, Blue Sedge, Tussock Bunchgrass and the rare Fen Orchid.

m1.title: The question
m1.intro: Dawn at Ashcombe Meadow. Your supervisor leaves one question on the station table: how abundant is Meadow Butterweed across the whole meadow? Before walking a single quadrat, look at the ground, choose a hypothesis, and check what you already know.
steps: Read the meadow facts and the research question.
Choose your hypothesis about how Butterweed is spread.

m2.title: Know your species
m2.intro: You cannot count what you cannot name. Study the five species in the field guide — shape and size first, colour second — then take the identification quiz (8 items). Misidentification later will show up in the reveal as an error source, so learn the marks now.
m2.guideCallout: Field marks are listed shape → size → leaf → colour. The models exaggerate marks slightly so they stay readable in the counting view.

m3.title: Fieldwork
m3.intro: Choose a sampling design, place your 10 quadrats within its rules, and record what is inside each one. You have a time budget: walking costs time, and the day ends when the meter runs out — there is no failing grade, only data you will defend in the reveal.
workflow: Pick a design on the map (each is described honestly, including the biased one).
Place quadrats: the design generates or constrains the points; walking between them costs time.
In each quadrat: switch to the top-down counting view, identify species with the field guide, enter counts (and a cover band for Bunchgrass).
Review the data sheet, then submit.

m4.title: The reveal
m4.intro: The meadow's true population, your estimate beside it, and the re-sampling simulator: 1,000 virtual repeats of your fieldwork at any sample size from 5 to 40 quadrats. Read the sampling distributions, then answer the interpretation items.
m4.simulatorBlurb: Each virtual sample uses the same design you chose, draws n quadrats, counts the true plants inside them, and computes the density estimate the way you did. The pile of 1,000 estimates is the sampling distribution.

m5.title: Report and transfer
m5.intro: Write your methods-and-results report from your own data, check it against the rubric, then carry the reasoning out of the meadow: the same logic of random, stratified and convenience sampling governs survey research.
m5.transferIntro: A school survey about study habits uses the same machinery as your quadrat survey: define the population, choose a fair design, report uncertainty, name the bias you could not remove.

sections.title: Sampling design
sections.guidance: Which design did you choose and why does it fit the question and this meadow? Name one alternative and why you rejected it.

sections.title: Results
sections.guidance: Your density estimates per species (individuals per m²) from your own data sheet, and the Bunchgrass cover estimate.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.guidance: Use the simulator: state the spread of estimates for your design and n (SD and a 95% interval from the percentiles), and say what it means.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.guidance: What did your design miss (compare with the reveal), what could you have misidentified, and what would you change?

report.note: Free-text answers are saved to your local learning record and are never graded automatically. The rubric self-check is for you.

revealErrorSources.label: Design bias
revealErrorSources.text: Quadrat placement favored some ground over other ground (visible for the 'wherever looks interesting' design and for any run of bad luck). Bias shifts the centre of the sampling distribution.

revealErrorSources.label: Sampling variance
revealErrorSources.text: Even a fair design lands on different quadrats each repeat, so estimates spread around the truth. More quadrats narrow the spread.

revealErrorSources.label: Missed rarity
revealErrorSources.text: Species that are rare and clumped (Fen Orchid) are mostly invisible to small samples. '0 observed' is not '0 present'.

revealErrorSources.label: Misidentification
revealErrorSources.text: Counts of the wrong species propagate into both the false species' overestimate and the true species' underestimate.
